title: TightVNC Pre-Auth RCE Vulnerability Lets Hackers Execute Code on Windows PCs, PoC Released
summary: A TightVNC Viewer vulnerability can let attackers execute code on Windows PCs before a password prompt appears. Research credited to SeongJoon Cho of SSD Labs Korea includes proof-of-concept exploit code targeting TightVNC 2.8.88 x64. The attack uses a malicious VNC server to send screen data that corrupts the viewer’s memory. The affected component is the viewer, not simply any Windows machine running a TightVNC server. Attackers need either network access to a viewer in Listening Mode or a user who connects the viewer to an attacker-controlled server. The supplied disclosure does not establish active exploitation. The flaw begins when the server announces its screen size through the Remote Framebuffer protocol (RFB) . TightVNC calculates the memory needed to hold that screen, but converts the result into a 32-bit integer. Large dimensions cause the value to wrap around, leaving a smaller allocation than expected. In the reported example, a server announces a 32,768-by-32,769 screen using 32 bits per pixel. The viewer allocates only 128 KB while retaining dimensions representing more than 4 GB of pixel data. Later screen updates write outside that small buffer because the pointer calculation lacks a check against the allocated size. TightVNC Pre-Auth RCE Vulnerability The PoC turns this memory corruption into code execution. It first changes an outgoing buffer’s length to leak nearby memory, revealing addresses needed to bypass address randomization. It then redirects a function call and uses return-oriented programming, which reuses existing code, to launch a process through Windows’ CreateProcessW function. Listening Mode exposes the viewer on TCP port 5500 and, according to the disclosure, accepts incoming server connections without a password or IP restriction. An attacker who can reach that port can target the viewer directly. An outbound connection to a rogue support server creates another route, with exploitation occurring before authentication. These conditions differ from VNC connection hijacking that relies on weak passwords. They also differ from remote access tools disguised as installers , where users install legitimate software under pretenses. Here, the attack targets memory handling inside the viewer itself. The researchers say the vendor did not respond and patched the issue on October 3, 2026. However, TightVNC’s official release notices identify October 2 and October 5 security updates, so the exact fix date remains unclear. The vendor says versions 2.8.89 and 2.8.90 address Viewer security issues and recommends 2.8.90 for that branch. Administrators should update affected viewers, turn off unnecessary Listening Mode, restrict port 5500 to trusted systems, and avoid untrusted VNC servers. Network restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching the vulnerable viewer. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

title: Hackers Target 61 GitHub Repositories With Command Injection Attacks to Steal CI/CD Secrets
summary: Hackers targeted 61 public GitHub repositories in a coordinated command injection campaign designed to steal data from automated development systems. Radware researchers identified 83 malicious issues, pull requests, and comments posted on September 1, 2026, with evidence that injected commands executed inside two GitHub Actions workflows. The findings show how routine project discussions can become entry points into software build systems. According to Radware’s investigation, 77 malicious items appeared within about 43 minutes. Six more followed in a second wave lasting roughly two minutes. Targets included Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave Browser, MLflow, ToolJet, and PX4-Autopilot. Their inclusion does not mean every project was breached. The attack chain (source: Radware ) The campaign exploited workflows that placed user-controlled text directly into shell scripts. GitHub Actions can automatically respond when someone opens an issue, submits a pull request, or posts a comment. These tasks may check titles, assign labels, or send notifications. Hackers Target 61 GitHub Repositories Attackers placed Bash command substitution expressions, written as $(), inside that content. When a vulnerable workflow inserted the text into executable shell code, Bash treated the embedded expression as a command rather than ordinary text. Wrapping the inserted title in double quotes did not prevent execution. The payload ran env to collect environment variables, encoded the output with Base64, removed newline characters, and used curl to attempt an HTTP POST request. PX4/PX4-Autopilot — Pull Request #28488 (source : Radware ) Every verified payload pointed to 54.205.16[.]142 on port 8443, with a separate collection identifier for each attempt. Despite the port number, the connection used HTTP rather than HTTPS. The risk depended on what each job could access. Environment variables could contain service tokens, deployment credentials, or internal settings. GitHub Actions secrets are not automatically available to every workflow, so execution alone does not establish that sensitive credentials were stolen. Snouzy/workout-cool Issue #251, showing the command-injection payload in the Issue title (source : Radware ) In PX4-Autopilot, a pull request posing as a documentation correction carried the payload in its title. A title-checking workflow inserted that title into a Bash command invoking Python. Logs showed a command-substitution warning and returned content beginning with GIF89a, replacing the malicious expression. In Snouzy/workout-cool, an issue notification workflow inserted the attacker’s title directly into a Bash variable assignment. A warning tied to that line confirmed command substitution. A later Discord request failed because its body contained invalid JSON, although that failure did not prove successful data theft. Radware did not confirm stolen secrets, repository write access, source code changes, or compromised releases. Researchers also found signs that some participating accounts may have been hijacked, including one owner publicly denying opening a malicious issue. The findings complement earlier reporting on GhostAction credential theft and the tj-actions supply chain attack . Those incidents used different routes but also put CI/CD secrets at risk. Account-owner comments denying authorship of the Issue and reporting subsequent account-protection actions (source : Radware) Maintainers should pass untrusted titles through environment variables instead of inserting them into shell source, avoid eval, and limit workflow permissions. Teams finding execution evidence should review available secrets, rotate potentially exposed credentials, inspect audit logs, and investigate unexpected outbound traffic. Keep notification jobs separate from privileged release workflows to reduce the damage an injected command could cause. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. title: Hackers Drain Bitcoin Hot Wallets on BTCPay Servers, Users Urged to Shut Down Immediately
summary: BTCPay Server has issued an urgent warning after receiving reports that attackers were draining Bitcoin hot wallets on its servers. The open-source payment processor told operators to shut down their installations immediately and keep them offline while its team investigates the thefts. The alert raises concerns for merchants holding funds in wallets managed through affected servers. In its November 1 security notice, the project said: “We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers.” It instructed operators to run ./btcpay-down.sh until the investigation is complete. The warning did not limit that instruction to specific software versions or announce that restarting was safe. We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers. If you're running an instance, please shut it down (./btcpay-down.sh) until we complete the investigation. — BTCPay Server (@BtcpayServer) November 1, 2026 BTCPay Server Warns Early findings point toward outdated installations. Founder Nicolas Dorier reportedly said affected servers were running versions older than 2.4.2 and that attackers had logged in as administrators. However, investigators had not established how they gained that access, leaving the initial entry point unconfirmed. Dorier also said the project’s public servers running version 2.4.7 had not been attacked. That observation is important, but it does not prove every updated installation is safe. Operators should not treat the absence of reported attacks against those servers as an all-clear while the broader shutdown warning remains in place. The available reports did not provide a confirmed loss total or a count of affected installations. No complete technical account has established whether the attackers used stolen login details, a software flaw, or another route to administrator access. BTCPay Server lets merchants accept Bitcoin directly using self-hosted software. Its wallet documentation explains that an enabled hot wallet signs transactions using a seed stored on the server. This makes payments convenient, but places sensitive signing material inside the online environment. A server breach can therefore put funds at risk, depending on the access obtained. The incident highlights risks also covered in Cyber Security News reporting on fake crypto wallet screens stealing recovery phrases and Google Sheets campaigns that swap wallet addresses . Those campaigns involve different methods, and neither has been linked to the BTCPay thefts. The shared concern is protecting wallet secrets and checking where funds are sent. Recent Patches Do Not Confirm the Cause The warning follows BTCPay Server 2.4.7, released October 29. Its official release notes list 85 security findings addressed after reports from Anthropic’s OSS Scanner program. These included one critical, 13 high, 52 medium, and 19 low-severity findings, covering permissions, authentication, payment handling, and other functions. There is no confirmed link between those fixes and the current wallet drains. A separate earlier advisory for version 2.4.2 concerned exposed Lightning Network Daemon credentials. BTCPay explicitly said its own on-chain wallets, including hot wallets, were not affected by that earlier issue. Combining the two incidents would misstate what developers have confirmed. For now, the clearest official action is to stop the server with ./btcpay-down.sh and leave it offline pending further guidance. Updating alone should not be presented as resolving an active compromise. Operators also need to distinguish confirmed developer instructions from community reports as the investigation develops and the team determines the attack path, affected deployments, and recovery steps.[ x ]

title: Inside a successful AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise to demonstrate independent operation
summary: On Saturday, October 24, 2026 we conducted a successful exercise demonstrating that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate without depending on any infrastructure outside the European Union (EU). This was the first public technical exercise demonstrating the independence of a sovereign cloud Region. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new, independent cloud partition for Europe that became generally available in January 2026, with its first AWS Region in Brandenburg, Germany. It is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions , with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and all customer content and customer-created metadata remains in the EU. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is managed through dedicated European legal entities established under German law and operated entirely within Europe. My fellow Managing Director, Stefan Hoechbauer, and I called for the exercise. We are EU citizens residing in the EU, responsible for its management and operations, including its infrastructure, technology, and services. Only EU residents located in the EU control its operations and support, and AWS is gradually transitioning the AWS European Sovereign Cloud to be operated exclusively by EU citizens located in the EU. What we did In standard operations, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud uses two global systems: the AWS Global Network backbone, and a dedicated system operated by the local EU team to manage limited, controlled transfers of operational AWS data. As we explained ahead of the exercise , neither is critical to running the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. During the exercise, the team switched off both systems, and traffic that normally travels across the AWS Global Network backbone rerouted securely over the public internet. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate independently at any time, and for several hours on October 24 the team showed exactly that, running it on only its own software and hardware resources, operated by EU-resident staff within the EU. Workloads continued running, and customers could still access their data. The exercise did not affect service availability within the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, other AWS Regions, or private connectivity through AWS Direct Connect . When the exercise finished, traffic returned to its normal path. Why we ran it Transparency is at the core of our digital sovereignty commitment, so we ran the AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise openly and reported back on the outcome. The exercise produced verifiable technical and operational evidence that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can continue to operate independently within the EU. It turns a design claim into a verified result. Organizations in regulated industries and the public sector can take this result to regulators and their boards as evidence for their compliance and assurance documents. What customers and partners are saying “Digital sovereignty is ultimately about trust and safeguarding business continuity. The successful demonstration of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud’s operational independence is an important proof point for European organizations with the most stringent sovereignty requirements. Combined with Capgemini’s European heritage, presence and AWS capabilities, we can deliver a sovereign proposition in Europe, for Europe, by Europeans, enabling clients to accelerate secure and resilient cloud and AI transformation at scale whilst assuring business continuity.” – Fernando Alvarez, Chief Strategy and Development Officer and Group Executive Board Member, Capgemini “Autonomy, resilience and operational control are foundations driving digital sovereignty concerns across the public sector and regulated industries. Achieving sovereignty requires more than a sound and consistent architecture; it demands operational evidence to build trust. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud team has provided evidence, supporting organizations on the transformation of their critical data and digital assets toward greater sovereign control. Having engaged with this team since the inception of the project, and as a Launch Partner of the AWS Digital Sovereignty Competency, Atos helps customers define their sovereignty roadmaps, adopt the appropriate graduated solutions, and confidently operate and govern their target sovereignty posture.” – Michael Kollar, Digital Sovereignty Leader and Head of Cloud & Modern Infrastructure and Digital Workplace, Atos Group “For organizations in regulated industries, meeting strict data and operational requirements cannot come at the cost of a great customer experience. Running on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, Genesys can help European organizations deliver exactly that, with their data and operations kept in the EU. Seeing the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operate independently under real conditions helps give our shared customers added confidence to move their most sensitive workloads to the cloud.” – Daniel Karadza, Senior Director, Partners and Alliances, EMEA Central and Benelux, Genesys “Operational independence is a defining pillar of digital sovereignty, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud has shown what that means in practice. It runs without reliance on any infrastructure outside the EU and is operated entirely by EU residents, which makes it a strong fit for Europe’s regulated industries and public sector. As an early collaborator with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud team before its launch, Accenture is uniquely positioned to help clients navigate sovereignty requirements and scale with greater confidence and control.” – Emanuele Baldassarre, Managing Director, Accenture Learn more To learn more about the design and digital sovereignty controls of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, visit aws.eu . If you have questions about this exercise or want to discuss your workloads, reach out to AWS Support or contact your AWS Account team. Stéphane Israël Stéphane is the leader and Managing Director of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. He is responsible for the management and operations of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, including infrastructure, technology, and services, in addition to broader digital sovereignty efforts at AWS. Prior to AWS, he was the CEO of Arianespace, where he oversaw numerous successful space missions, including the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope.

title: Critical Certificate Validation Flaw in LXD and Incus Could Give Hackers Control of Linux Hosts
summary: A critical certificate validation flaw in LXD and Incus could let remote attackers bypass login checks and take control of clusters and managed virtual machines. The weakness affects the HTTPS management listener, placing exposed Linux systems at risk without requiring a password, stolen private key, or user interaction. Incus rates its flaw critical, with a CVSS score of 10.0. The Incus security advisory , published on October 29, says the bug has existed since the project’s initial release. Canonical published its related LXD record, CVE-2026-112816, on October 30. Although Ubuntu assigns that record Medium priority, it describes an unauthenticated path to full cluster and virtual machine access. Certificate Validation Flaw in LXD and Incus The problem lies in how the service checks certificates presented during an HTTPS connection. The TLS handshake proves that a client holds the private key for the first certificate it submits. However, the remaining certificates in that chain are controlled by the client and are not verified. Authentication checks then compare every certificate in the submitted chain against the server’s trust store. This creates a gap between proving ownership of a certificate and accepting its identity. An attacker can append a trusted certificate’s public part to their own chain and be accepted as its owner, despite lacking the matching private key. Public certificates are not secrets. Servers return their certificates during TLS handshakes, meaning an attacker needs no existing account to obtain one. According to the advisory, presenting the server’s own certificate grants database gateway access, while presenting another cluster member’s certificate grants internal cluster access and bypasses authorization entirely. This differs from the container escape flaws covered in Cyber Security News’ runc vulnerability report . Rather than breaking out of an isolated workload, this bug targets the trusted management layer that controls access to the environment. The Incus advisory says attackers can impersonate trusted client, metrics, or server certificates when they have the relevant public certificate. The same weakness allows renewal or deletion of trust store entries through self-service paths. It also affects authentication for the agent connection between hosts and virtual machines. Another affected area is the authorization scriptlet, a script used to make access decisions. Incus passed the unverified certificate chain to this script, allowing attacker-chosen certificates to influence its decisions. This also affects connections using tokens or OpenID Connect, because those clients can still present certificates during the handshake. Fixed Versions and Immediate Protection Incus lists versions before 7.6.0 as affected and version 7.6.0 onward as patched. Canonical’s LXD notice identifies fixes in versions 4.0.15, 5.0.11, 5.21.9, and 6.10.1 for the affected release branches. Administrators should check their installed version against the relevant vendor advisory. Until updates are applied, Incus advises restricting HTTPS listener access to trusted hosts. There is no configuration-based workaround that fixes the underlying validation error. Network restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching. Cyber Security News’ Linux container security guide provides broader context on protecting container environments. For this flaw, the immediate focus is narrower: update affected services and limit who can reach their management interfaces. Neither cited advisory reports active exploitation, so exposure should not be confused with confirmed compromise. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

The problem lies in how the service checks certificates presented during an HTTPS connection. The TLS handshake proves that a client holds the private key for the first certificate it submits. However, the remaining certificates in that chain are controlled by the client and are not verified.

Authentication checks then compare every certificate in the submitted chain against the server’s trust store. This creates a gap between proving ownership of a certificate and accepting its identity. An attacker can append a trusted certificate’s public part to their own chain and be accepted as its owner, despite lacking the matching private key.

Public certificates are not secrets. Servers return their certificates during TLS handshakes, meaning an attacker needs no existing account to obtain one. According to the advisory, presenting the server’s own certificate grants database gateway access, while presenting another cluster member’s certificate grants internal cluster access and bypasses authorization entirely.

This differs from the container escape flaws covered in Cyber Security News’ runc vulnerability report. Rather than breaking out of an isolated workload, this bug targets the trusted management layer that controls access to the environment.

The Incus advisory says attackers can impersonate trusted client, metrics, or server certificates when they have the relevant public certificate. The same weakness allows renewal or deletion of trust store entries through self-service paths. It also affects authentication for the agent connection between hosts and virtual machines.

Another affected area is the authorization scriptlet, a script used to make access decisions. Incus passed the unverified certificate chain to this script, allowing attacker-chosen certificates to influence its decisions. This also affects connections using tokens or OpenID Connect, because those clients can still present certificates during the handshake.

Fixed Versions and Immediate Protection

Incus lists versions before 7.6.0 as affected and version 7.6.0 onward as patched. Canonical’s LXD notice identifies fixes in versions 4.0.15, 5.0.11, 5.21.9, and 6.10.1 for the affected release branches. Administrators should check their installed version against the relevant vendor advisory.

Until updates are applied, Incus advises restricting HTTPS listener access to trusted hosts. There is no configuration-based workaround that fixes the underlying validation error. Network restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Cyber Security News’ Linux container security guide provides broader context on protecting container environments. For this flaw, the immediate focus is narrower: update affected services and limit who can reach their management interfaces. Neither cited advisory reports active exploitation, so exposure should not be confused with confirmed compromise.

title: Frida 17.25.1 Released
summary: Fallout from the new mapper, reported within days by @Albasha0x0 on Windows and @quakquak86 on Android, along with a reorganization of our repositories on GitHub. Android Attaching to a Unity game on Android 16 crashed the target, trying to execute non-executable memory in libc. A process may map a library file on its own, outside of the dynamic linker, and when such a mapping came before the loaded image, the mapper used it as the library’s base and bound imports into memory that was never executable. Each library’s base is now picked through the same lookup that prefers the mapping the linker actually loaded. Thanks for the thorough A/B report, quakquak86! The same device turned up a second problem. An agent mapped by our mapper is unknown to Bionic, which attributes its dlsym() calls to the anonymous namespace. In an untrusted app that namespace is isolated, so RTLD_DEFAULT couldn’t see libc, and the agent aborted on startup. We now resolve libc through the unrestricted linker API, using our own import of open() as the trusted caller rather than something obtained from dlsym() , which suffers from the same problem. Windows Albasha0x0 noticed that a .NET program’s main assembly went missing from Process.enumerateModules() , and never showed up through the module observer either. The loader doesn’t send DLL notifications for images that lack the IMAGE_FILE_DLL characteristic, and that is how CoreCLR loads the main assembly, through LoadLibrary() . The LdrLoadDll() and LdrUnloadDll() hooks are now kept alongside the notifications, and the registry synchronizes when either returns. They also found that an attached program crashed at exit. When a process exits, its other threads are terminated before DLL detach notifications run, including the agent’s. The injector then saw its thread end without the agent having asked to stay resident, and unmapped it while hooks such as the unwind broker’s were still in place, so anything running during the rest of the shutdown, like the compatibility shim engine walking the stack, called into unmapped memory. The agent is now left mapped when the process is already exiting. Thanks for both reports! Processes running with Arbitrary Code Guard delegate their code memory to the host, and tearing down the module registry there could abort, as reverting its loader hooks patches code and the memory hooks needed for that were gone by the time final destructors ran. The registry is now torn down in gum_shutdown() , which the agent calls as the last step of removing instrumentation, while the host connection is still up. GitHub The frida organization on GitHub had grown to the point where Frida itself sat next to patched forks of GLib and V8, npm packages, and demos and conference material going back a decade. It has been split into four: frida is Frida itself: the runtime, tools, language bindings, and the Luma GUI. frida-packages holds the packages you build on: runtime bridges such as frida-java-bridge and frida-objc-bridge, agent tooling like frida-compile and frida-itrace, and the Node.js compatibility modules published as @frida/ . frida-forks is our patched forks of third-party projects. It is not a list of Frida’s dependencies, as which forks a build uses depends on the platform and configuration, and some are only used by tooling or by Luma. frida-labs has the experiments, proof-of-concept apps, demos, and conference material, with the retired ones archived for reference. GitHub redirects the old URLs, but ours have all been updated, and the release engineering tooling now supports dependencies hosted outside the frida organization. For distro packaging, Efni and Idun now build against GLib older than 2.84, and Idun falls back to its bundled libusb when the system one is older than 1.0.30. Enjoy! Changelog linux: Ignore library mappings made outside the dynamic linker when picking a library’s base in the mapper. Thanks @quakquak86 ! linux: Look up libc through the unrestricted linker API on Android, as Bionic isolates mapped agents in untrusted apps. Thanks @quakquak86 ! windows: Register images that the loader doesn’t send DLL notifications for, such as a .NET program’s main assembly. Thanks @Albasha0x0 ! windows: Keep the agent mapped while the target exits, fixing a crash at exit. Thanks @Albasha0x0 ! windows: Tear down the module registry while patching still works, fixing an abort on unload in processes with Arbitrary Code Guard. windows: Include winternl.h for NTSTATUS , fixing the build with recent SDKs. linux: Add a test checking that spawn leaves SIGCHLD alone. Thanks @leonitousconforti ! efni: Support GLib older than 2.84. idun: Support GLib older than 2.84, and fall back to the bundled libusb when the system one is older than 1.0.30. releng: Support dependencies hosted outside the frida organization, and point at the forks’ new home in frida-forks .
summary_html:
Fallout from the new mapper, reported within days by @Albasha0x0 on Windows and @quakquak86 on Android, along with a reorganization of our repositories on GitHub.

Android

Attaching to a Unity game on Android 16 crashed the target, trying to execute non-executable memory in libc. A process may map a library file on its own, outside of the dynamic linker, and when such a mapping came before the loaded image, the mapper used it as the library’s base and bound imports into memory that was never executable. Each library’s base is now picked through the same lookup that prefers the mapping the linker actually loaded. Thanks for the thorough A/B report, quakquak86!

The same device turned up a second problem. An agent mapped by our mapper is unknown to Bionic, which attributes its dlsym() calls to the anonymous namespace. In an untrusted app that namespace is isolated, so RTLD_DEFAULT couldn’t see libc, and the agent aborted on startup. We now resolve libc through the unrestricted linker API, using our own import of open() as the trusted caller rather than something obtained from dlsym(), which suffers from the same problem.

Windows

Albasha0x0 noticed that a .NET program’s main assembly went missing from Process.enumerateModules(), and never showed up through the module observer either. The loader doesn’t send DLL notifications for images that lack the IMAGE_FILE_DLL characteristic, and that is how CoreCLR loads the main assembly, through LoadLibrary(). The LdrLoadDll() and LdrUnloadDll() hooks are now kept alongside the notifications, and the registry synchronizes when either returns.

They also found that an attached program crashed at exit. When a process exits, its other threads are terminated before DLL detach notifications run, including the agent’s. The injector then saw its thread end without the agent having asked to stay resident, and unmapped it while hooks such as the unwind broker’s were still in place, so anything running during the rest of the shutdown, like the compatibility shim engine walking the stack, called into unmapped memory. The agent is now left mapped when the process is already exiting. Thanks for both reports!

Processes running with Arbitrary Code Guard delegate their code memory to the host, and tearing down the module registry there could abort, as reverting its loader hooks patches code and the memory hooks needed for that were gone by the time final destructors ran. The registry is now torn down in gum_shutdown(), which the agent calls as the last step of removing instrumentation, while the host connection is still up.

GitHub

The frida organization on GitHub had grown to the point where Frida itself sat next to patched forks of GLib and V8, npm packages, and demos and conference material going back a decade. It has been split into four:

  • frida is Frida itself: the runtime, tools, language bindings, and the Luma GUI.
  • frida-packages holds the packages you build on: runtime bridges such as frida-java-bridge and frida-objc-bridge, agent tooling like frida-compile and frida-itrace, and the Node.js compatibility modules published as @frida/.
  • frida-forks is our patched forks of third-party projects. It is not a list of Frida’s dependencies, as which forks a build uses depends on the platform and configuration, and some are only used by tooling or by Luma.
  • frida-labs has the experiments, proof-of-concept apps, demos, and conference material, with the retired ones archived for reference.

GitHub redirects the old URLs, but ours have all been updated, and the release engineering tooling now supports dependencies hosted outside the frida organization.

For distro packaging, Efni and Idun now build against GLib older than 2.84, and Idun falls back to its bundled libusb when the system one is older than 1.0.30.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • linux: Ignore library mappings made outside the dynamic linker when picking a library’s base in the mapper. Thanks @quakquak86!
  • linux: Look up libc through the unrestricted linker API on Android, as Bionic isolates mapped agents in untrusted apps. Thanks @quakquak86!
  • windows: Register images that the loader doesn’t send DLL notifications for, such as a .NET program’s main assembly. Thanks @Albasha0x0!
  • windows: Keep the agent mapped while the target exits, fixing a crash at exit. Thanks @Albasha0x0!
  • windows: Tear down the module registry while patching still works, fixing an abort on unload in processes with Arbitrary Code Guard.
  • windows: Include winternl.h for NTSTATUS, fixing the build with recent SDKs.
  • linux: Add a test checking that spawn leaves SIGCHLD alone. Thanks @leonitousconforti!
  • efni: Support GLib older than 2.84.
  • idun: Support GLib older than 2.84, and fall back to the bundled libusb when the system one is older than 1.0.30.
  • releng: Support dependencies hosted outside the frida organization, and point at the forks’ new home in frida-forks.

title: Modern Authentication, Legacy Problems
summary: Introduction During a recent incident response investigation, we encountered an interesting authentication issue in an on-premises Microsoft Exchange environment. The organization had implemented Hybrid Modern Authentication (HMA), allowing Microsoft Outlook to authenticate against Microsoft Entra ID using OAuth tokens. Multi-factor authentication was enforced through the organization’s Microsoft 365 configuration. However, while investigating the Exchange logs, we found thousands of successfully authenticated EWS requests from another client using NTLM . How could NTLM authentication still succeed when the organization had implemented Hybrid Modern Authentication and required MFA? The answer was an externally accessible legacy authentication path that operated independently of Microsoft Entra ID.
summary_html:
Introduction

During a recent incident response investigation, we encountered an interesting authentication issue in an on-premises Microsoft Exchange environment. The organization had implemented Hybrid Modern Authentication (HMA), allowing Microsoft Outlook to authenticate against Microsoft Entra ID using OAuth tokens. Multi-factor authentication was enforced through the organization’s Microsoft 365 configuration. However, while investigating the Exchange logs, we found thousands of successfully authenticated EWS requests from another client using NTLM.

How could NTLM authentication still succeed when the organization had implemented Hybrid Modern Authentication and required MFA? The answer was an externally accessible legacy authentication path that operated independently of Microsoft Entra ID.

title: FBI Confirms North Korean Hackers Responsible for $6 Billion+ Binance Attack
summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation has confirmed that North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance on or about October 29, 2026. The agency tracks the activity as TraderTraitor, linking the cryptocurrency theft to an operation previously blamed for major attacks against digital asset platforms. In its official security alert, the FBI said investigators observed the attackers converting stolen funds primarily into Ethereum. The investigation involves the United States Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service’s Criminal Investigation division, bringing together agencies focused on cybercrime, financial fraud, and illicit money flows. Binance estimated the financial impact at approximately $6.3 billion. Its initial investigation suggested that a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer may have enabled unauthorized withdrawals. The company later identified additional breach points, meaning the full attack path remains under investigation rather than established as a single device compromise. FBI Confirms North Korean Hackers Cybersecurity News previously reported on the Binance cryptocurrency theft, citing TRM Labs findings that wallets across ten blockchains were drained, with most funds moved within roughly 20 minutes. Researchers also identified malicious sweeper contract activity targeting an Ethereum hot wallet, a wallet used for online transactions. These findings describe how funds were removed, but they do not establish exactly how the attackers first entered Binance’s systems. The FBI alert does not identify an exploited vulnerability, a malware family, or a complete technical chain. Claims that a specific software flaw caused the breach therefore remain unsupported by that notice. The FBI expects the stolen assets to move through decentralized finance, or DeFi, platforms and instant swap services during further laundering stages. These services allow digital assets to be exchanged, potentially creating additional transfers that investigators must follow. The observed Ethereum conversions are confirmed activity, while the next laundering steps remain the agency’s assessment. Authorities are urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, DeFi providers, THORNode operators, and remote procedure call node operators to block transactions involving addresses used by the attackers. The request also covers transactions derived from those addresses, extending attention beyond the wallets that initially received stolen assets. TraderTraitor has a documented history of cryptocurrency theft. The FBI previously attributed the approximately $1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025 to the same activity. Cybersecurity News’s Bybit attack investigation coverage described developer workstation compromise, cloud access, and changes to a wallet interface. Those findings provide background, not proof that Binance suffered the same attack chain. According to reports, Binance said it had covered 95% of the stolen tokens and planned to restore withdrawals in phases on November 1. The remaining assets were less liquid and harder to source. Replacing customer assets should not be confused with recovering the funds held by the attackers. Anyone with relevant information can contact an FBI field office or submit a report through the Internet Crime Complaint Center . IC3 collects cybercrime reports to support investigations and identify patterns. It also warns that it does not partner with private crypto recovery services, an important caution for victims approached with promises to recover stolen funds. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

title: Hacktober – Cyberattack Wave Hits PHP, Node.js, Binance, LiteLLM, Pentagon, and a Few More
summary: October brought a heavy run of cybersecurity disclosures involving cryptocurrency exchanges, web servers, AI tools, software packages, government records, and grocery chains. Binance investigated billions of dollars in unauthorized transactions, PHP issued emergency fixes, and a malicious LiteLLM release put developer credentials at risk. Other incidents involved Railway, OpenCode, Polymarket, Coinbase, Cursor, eMudhra, and Capcom. Together, these reports show how exposed credentials and trusted software channels can turn a limited intrusion into a much larger security problem. The name “Hacktober” captures the volume of news, but it should not suggest that every event belonged to one coordinated campaign. The reports cover different attack methods, discovery dates, and levels of confirmation. Some describe confirmed data theft; others involve possible exposure, malicious packages, or vulnerabilities that could enable an attack. Keeping those categories separate is essential to understanding what happened and who actually faced risk. Binance Investigates Multibillion-Dollar Wallet Drain Binance became the largest financial story in the roundup after suspending deposits and withdrawals during a security investigation. Cybersecurity News’ updated Binance breach report placed the estimated incident impact at $6.3 billion and reported that around $3 billion had been frozen through blockchain partners. These figures require careful wording. The total associated with suspicious transactions is not necessarily the final amount permanently lost, particularly while investigators are tracing funds and arranging freezes. Early findings reportedly pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop. Attackers may have used that access to reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals. Binance said it had not found evidence that wallet private keys were leaked and stated that it would cover losses. That separates the reported attack from a simple private-key theft scenario. Systems that prepare, authorize, or process transactions can become targets even when the signing keys themselves remain protected. The scale could place the event among the largest cryptocurrency thefts reported, but describing it as the largest completed heist requires a settled loss figure. Investigators still needed to distinguish unauthorized outflows, frozen assets, recovered funds, and the amount ultimately left unrecovered. Polymarket Wallet Theft and Coinbase Vendor Exposure Polymarket faced a separate incident involving its international platform. According to Cybersecurity News’ Polymarket coverage , malicious JavaScript searched browser storage for trading credentials and attempted to reach an active trading client. Outside analysis connected at least $2.7 million in withdrawals to 710 wallets, although Polymarket had not confirmed that total. The reported behavior placed browser-held credentials and active sessions at the center of the investigation. Coinbase’s disclosure involved a different type of exposure. Its analytics provider, Amplitude, experienced a security incident that exposed some customer contact information. Coinbase said its own systems and customer funds were not affected. The Coinbase vendor incident report therefore should not be described as another exchange wallet drain. Its main concern was customer information held by a third party, rather than confirmed access to cryptocurrency balances. PHP2Shell Creates an Urgent Web Server Patching Problem PHP2Shell became a major concern for web administrators because it involved two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both received severity scores of 9.2. Reporting described memory-handling flaws that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on affected servers under vulnerable configurations. Researchers demonstrated an attack path involving Apache’s mod_php module before normal application code ran. The PHP emergency patch report listed fixed releases including PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. This made the underlying runtime, rather than only the website’s application code, the focus of remediation. A site could use an updated content management system and still remain exposed if its PHP installation was vulnerable. Running workers also needed to load the corrected build before the update could provide protection. The attack timeline added urgency, but it also required precision. AWS reported exploitation attempts before public disclosure. Later reporting distinguished scanning and failed attempts from evidence of successful compromise in another observed environment. Cybersecurity News’ PHP2Shell exploit analysis explains why public exploit availability, attempted exploitation, and confirmed server compromise should not be treated as the same finding. Node.js Updates Add to the Developer Workload Node.js security updates arrived alongside the PHP emergency, increasing the workload for teams responsible for public-facing applications and development infrastructure. The October 21 security roundup described ten Node.js vulnerabilities, including four rated high severity. Reported issues involved Brotli decompression memory corruption, TLS hostname validation, and DNS handling. Patched releases listed in the coverage included Node.js 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4. For organizations using containers, the relevant version was the runtime inside the deployed image. Updating a development laptop or a server’s default Node.js installation would not automatically replace an older runtime bundled into a separate application image. The combined PHP and Node.js disclosures made runtime inventories an important part of the response. LiteLLM Turns a Trusted Update Into a Credential Threat The LiteLLM supply-chain compromise showed how a software update could become the initial entry point. Version 1.107.0 reportedly reached PyPI with a credential stealer and remote access malware across all seven wheel files. Affected container tags extended the exposure beyond users who installed the Python package directly. The malicious code searched for cloud credentials, SSH keys, browser information, and AI service tokens. Python startup hooks made the attack particularly concerning because execution did not depend on an application explicitly importing LiteLLM. A routine Python command inside a contaminated environment could activate the payload. That widened the risk to build jobs and maintenance tasks that might not appear directly connected to the affected application. Reporting linked the compromised release to stolen GitHub credentials and a workflow redirected toward a lookalike repository. Stolen AWS credentials were reportedly used within roughly four and a half hours. A downgrade alone would not reverse that exposure. Recovery required treating credentials available to the affected environment as potentially stolen, alongside replacing contaminated software and rebuilding from a trusted source. GitHub Actions, npm, and Cursor Highlight Supply-Chain Weaknesses The statement “GitHub Actions got hacked” needs a narrower explanation. Cybersecurity News reported that the GhostAction campaign placed malicious workflows in 790 repositories. Those workflows put cloud credentials, software publishing tokens, and AI service keys at risk. The GhostAction investigation described abuse of repository automation, not proof that GitHub’s central platform had been breached. npm reporting also covered different categories of risk. An October disclosure described a trusted-publishing weakness that exposed more than 1,500 packages to possible takeover. That finding should not be converted into a claim that every affected package had already delivered malware. The npm trusted-publishing report concerned an attack opportunity, which is distinct from a confirmed malicious release. Cursor separately confirmed that malicious Claude Code extension packages had appeared in its extension marketplace. The Cursor marketplace report demonstrated another trusted delivery route that attackers could abuse. The relevant issue was the distribution of malicious extension packages, rather than evidence that every Cursor installation or the entire editor codebase was compromised. Railway and OpenCode Face Stored-Secret Exposure Railway disclosed possible unauthorized access to customer environment variables, including some decrypted values. Such variables may contain database passwords, cloud tokens, registry credentials, and AI provider keys. The company paused deployments during its investigation and advised customers to rotate secrets. Its security incident disclosure described possible exposure, not a confirmed theft of every customer’s configuration. OpenCode said its breach affected 1.4% of Console users, including some workspaces with linked external providers. Unauthorized access to a legacy system may have exposed third-party API keys. The OpenCode breach report matters because the percentage applies to the identified Console population, not automatically to every person using the open-source coding tool. These incidents illustrate why the scope of a secret store matters. A single affected platform may hold credentials that unlock services operated by several other companies. The initial breach and any later misuse of those keys remain separate events, even when they share the same starting point. Fireworks AI, TiDB Cloud, and Warp Require Careful Scope Fireworks AI, TiDB Cloud, and Warp also appeared in October’s developer-platform incident reporting. However, the available research for this article did not establish matching Cybersecurity News reports for all three. Their inclusion should not become a blanket claim that every customer model, hosted database, or development session was accessed. The same reporting rule applies across this roundup. Exposure of internal credentials, management records, or vendor-held logs does not automatically establish theft of the main service’s complete customer dataset. Where the requested publication does not provide a verified account, detailed claims should remain outside the article rather than being presented as confirmed facts. eMudhra’s Certificate Problem Threatens Browser Trust The eMudhra certificate authority disclosure involved eight intermediate certificate authority private keys that were recoverable because of weak key generation. Reporting described extremely small private values, making recovery possible almost immediately. Browser and operating system vendors moved to block the affected certificates. This was not established as a conventional intrusion into eMudhra’s network. The company said its infrastructure had not been compromised and that the affected intermediate authorities had issued no end-entity certificates. It later announced its exit from the global SSL/TLS certificate business. The follow-up coverage underlines the distinction between a recoverable cryptographic key and a confirmed network breach. Both can create serious trust problems, but they arise differently. Pentagon and Denmark Disclosures Expose Sensitive Records The Pentagon personnel data breach reportedly affected more than three million people, including around 2.76 million living individuals and 294,000 deceased people. Unauthorized access reportedly occurred between October 2025 and July 2026 through a file-sharing vulnerability. The disclosure therefore belongs in the wider wave of security news, but the intrusion itself did not begin in October 2026. Denmark’s separate incident involved approximately 8.8 million registered people. According to Cybersecurity News’ Denmark breach coverage , the access involved misuse of a private company’s permitted connection to population records. The total included deceased people and people living abroad, explaining why it exceeded the country’s current population. These details are necessary to avoid presenting the figure as 8.8 million current residents. Capcom, SoftBank, and Grocery Systems Broaden the Impact Capcom disclosed exposure involving 11,774,247 customer records in its CAPCOM ID incident report . SoftBank also appeared in breach discussions, but its documented third-party data exposure dated to June 2025 and affected 137,000 users. That older event should not be repackaged as a newly confirmed October breach of SoftBank’s entire network. Retail reporting showed that cyber incidents can disrupt operations as well as expose records. Ahold Delhaize took some systems offline after identifying a security issue, according to its October incident coverage . Reports of remotely disrupted French supermarket refrigeration added another operational concern, although this research did not identify matching Cybersecurity News coverage suitable for linking here. Across the verified cases, scope remains the most important reporting detail. A malicious package is not the same as a compromised registry, a vendor breach is not automatically a breach of every customer system, and an estimated cryptocurrency outflow is not a final loss figure. Those distinctions make the October wave more understandable without making its impact any less serious. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

October brought a heavy run of cybersecurity disclosures involving cryptocurrency exchanges, web servers, AI tools, software packages, government records, and grocery chains.

Binance investigated billions of dollars in unauthorized transactions, PHP issued emergency fixes, and a malicious LiteLLM release put developer credentials at risk.

Other incidents involved Railway, OpenCode, Polymarket, Coinbase, Cursor, eMudhra, and Capcom. Together, these reports show how exposed credentials and trusted software channels can turn a limited intrusion into a much larger security problem.

The name “Hacktober” captures the volume of news, but it should not suggest that every event belonged to one coordinated campaign. The reports cover different attack methods, discovery dates, and levels of confirmation.

Some describe confirmed data theft; others involve possible exposure, malicious packages, or vulnerabilities that could enable an attack. Keeping those categories separate is essential to understanding what happened and who actually faced risk.

Binance Investigates Multibillion-Dollar Wallet Drain

Binance became the largest financial story in the roundup after suspending deposits and withdrawals during a security investigation. Cybersecurity News’ updated Binance breach report placed the estimated incident impact at $6.3 billion and reported that around $3 billion had been frozen through blockchain partners. These figures require careful wording.

The total associated with suspicious transactions is not necessarily the final amount permanently lost, particularly while investigators are tracing funds and arranging freezes.

Early findings reportedly pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop. Attackers may have used that access to reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals.

Binance said it had not found evidence that wallet private keys were leaked and stated that it would cover losses. That separates the reported attack from a simple private-key theft scenario. Systems that prepare, authorize, or process transactions can become targets even when the signing keys themselves remain protected.

The scale could place the event among the largest cryptocurrency thefts reported, but describing it as the largest completed heist requires a settled loss figure. Investigators still needed to distinguish unauthorized outflows, frozen assets, recovered funds, and the amount ultimately left unrecovered.

Polymarket Wallet Theft and Coinbase Vendor Exposure

Polymarket faced a separate incident involving its international platform. According to Cybersecurity News’ Polymarket coverage, malicious JavaScript searched browser storage for trading credentials and attempted to reach an active trading client. Outside analysis connected at least $2.7 million in withdrawals to 710 wallets, although Polymarket had not confirmed that total. The reported behavior placed browser-held credentials and active sessions at the center of the investigation.

Coinbase’s disclosure involved a different type of exposure. Its analytics provider, Amplitude, experienced a security incident that exposed some customer contact information. Coinbase said its own systems and customer funds were not affected. The Coinbase vendor incident report therefore should not be described as another exchange wallet drain. Its main concern was customer information held by a third party, rather than confirmed access to cryptocurrency balances.

PHP2Shell Creates an Urgent Web Server Patching Problem

PHP2Shell became a major concern for web administrators because it involved two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both received severity scores of 9.2. Reporting described memory-handling flaws that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on affected servers under vulnerable configurations. Researchers demonstrated an attack path involving Apache’s mod_php module before normal application code ran.

The PHP emergency patch report listed fixed releases including PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. This made the underlying runtime, rather than only the website’s application code, the focus of remediation. A site could use an updated content management system and still remain exposed if its PHP installation was vulnerable. Running workers also needed to load the corrected build before the update could provide protection.

The attack timeline added urgency, but it also required precision. AWS reported exploitation attempts before public disclosure. Later reporting distinguished scanning and failed attempts from evidence of successful compromise in another observed environment. Cybersecurity News’ PHP2Shell exploit analysis explains why public exploit availability, attempted exploitation, and confirmed server compromise should not be treated as the same finding.

Node.js Updates Add to the Developer Workload

Node.js security updates arrived alongside the PHP emergency, increasing the workload for teams responsible for public-facing applications and development infrastructure. The October 21 security roundup described ten Node.js vulnerabilities, including four rated high severity. Reported issues involved Brotli decompression memory corruption, TLS hostname validation, and DNS handling.

Patched releases listed in the coverage included Node.js 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4. For organizations using containers, the relevant version was the runtime inside the deployed image. Updating a development laptop or a server’s default Node.js installation would not automatically replace an older runtime bundled into a separate application image. The combined PHP and Node.js disclosures made runtime inventories an important part of the response.

LiteLLM Turns a Trusted Update Into a Credential Threat

The LiteLLM supply-chain compromise showed how a software update could become the initial entry point. Version 1.107.0 reportedly reached PyPI with a credential stealer and remote access malware across all seven wheel files. Affected container tags extended the exposure beyond users who installed the Python package directly.

The malicious code searched for cloud credentials, SSH keys, browser information, and AI service tokens. Python startup hooks made the attack particularly concerning because execution did not depend on an application explicitly importing LiteLLM. A routine Python command inside a contaminated environment could activate the payload. That widened the risk to build jobs and maintenance tasks that might not appear directly connected to the affected application.

Reporting linked the compromised release to stolen GitHub credentials and a workflow redirected toward a lookalike repository. Stolen AWS credentials were reportedly used within roughly four and a half hours. A downgrade alone would not reverse that exposure. Recovery required treating credentials available to the affected environment as potentially stolen, alongside replacing contaminated software and rebuilding from a trusted source.

GitHub Actions, npm, and Cursor Highlight Supply-Chain Weaknesses

The statement “GitHub Actions got hacked” needs a narrower explanation. Cybersecurity News reported that the GhostAction campaign placed malicious workflows in 790 repositories. Those workflows put cloud credentials, software publishing tokens, and AI service keys at risk. The GhostAction investigation described abuse of repository automation, not proof that GitHub’s central platform had been breached.

npm reporting also covered different categories of risk. An October disclosure described a trusted-publishing weakness that exposed more than 1,500 packages to possible takeover. That finding should not be converted into a claim that every affected package had already delivered malware. The npm trusted-publishing report concerned an attack opportunity, which is distinct from a confirmed malicious release.

Cursor separately confirmed that malicious Claude Code extension packages had appeared in its extension marketplace. The Cursor marketplace report demonstrated another trusted delivery route that attackers could abuse. The relevant issue was the distribution of malicious extension packages, rather than evidence that every Cursor installation or the entire editor codebase was compromised.

Railway and OpenCode Face Stored-Secret Exposure

Railway disclosed possible unauthorized access to customer environment variables, including some decrypted values. Such variables may contain database passwords, cloud tokens, registry credentials, and AI provider keys. The company paused deployments during its investigation and advised customers to rotate secrets. Its security incident disclosure described possible exposure, not a confirmed theft of every customer’s configuration.

OpenCode said its breach affected 1.4% of Console users, including some workspaces with linked external providers. Unauthorized access to a legacy system may have exposed third-party API keys. The OpenCode breach report matters because the percentage applies to the identified Console population, not automatically to every person using the open-source coding tool.

These incidents illustrate why the scope of a secret store matters. A single affected platform may hold credentials that unlock services operated by several other companies. The initial breach and any later misuse of those keys remain separate events, even when they share the same starting point.

Fireworks AI, TiDB Cloud, and Warp Require Careful Scope

Fireworks AI, TiDB Cloud, and Warp also appeared in October’s developer-platform incident reporting. However, the available research for this article did not establish matching Cybersecurity News reports for all three. Their inclusion should not become a blanket claim that every customer model, hosted database, or development session was accessed.

The same reporting rule applies across this roundup. Exposure of internal credentials, management records, or vendor-held logs does not automatically establish theft of the main service’s complete customer dataset. Where the requested publication does not provide a verified account, detailed claims should remain outside the article rather than being presented as confirmed facts.

eMudhra’s Certificate Problem Threatens Browser Trust

The eMudhra certificate authority disclosure involved eight intermediate certificate authority private keys that were recoverable because of weak key generation. Reporting described extremely small private values, making recovery possible almost immediately. Browser and operating system vendors moved to block the affected certificates.

This was not established as a conventional intrusion into eMudhra’s network. The company said its infrastructure had not been compromised and that the affected intermediate authorities had issued no end-entity certificates. It later announced its exit from the global SSL/TLS certificate business. The follow-up coverage underlines the distinction between a recoverable cryptographic key and a confirmed network breach. Both can create serious trust problems, but they arise differently.

Pentagon and Denmark Disclosures Expose Sensitive Records

The Pentagon personnel data breach reportedly affected more than three million people, including around 2.76 million living individuals and 294,000 deceased people. Unauthorized access reportedly occurred between October 2025 and July 2026 through a file-sharing vulnerability. The disclosure therefore belongs in the wider wave of security news, but the intrusion itself did not begin in October 2026.

Denmark’s separate incident involved approximately 8.8 million registered people. According to Cybersecurity News’ Denmark breach coverage, the access involved misuse of a private company’s permitted connection to population records. The total included deceased people and people living abroad, explaining why it exceeded the country’s current population. These details are necessary to avoid presenting the figure as 8.8 million current residents.

Capcom, SoftBank, and Grocery Systems Broaden the Impact

Capcom disclosed exposure involving 11,774,247 customer records in its CAPCOM ID incident report. SoftBank also appeared in breach discussions, but its documented third-party data exposure dated to June 2025 and affected 137,000 users. That older event should not be repackaged as a newly confirmed October breach of SoftBank’s entire network.

Retail reporting showed that cyber incidents can disrupt operations as well as expose records. Ahold Delhaize took some systems offline after identifying a security issue, according to its October incident coverage.

Reports of remotely disrupted French supermarket refrigeration added another operational concern, although this research did not identify matching Cybersecurity News coverage suitable for linking here.

Across the verified cases, scope remains the most important reporting detail. A malicious package is not the same as a compromised registry, a vendor breach is not automatically a breach of every customer system, and an estimated cryptocurrency outflow is not a final loss figure. Those distinctions make the October wave more understandable without making its impact any less serious.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?
